questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish protocol or ethics approval, plan finalization, amendment effective dates, registry posting or update, data cutoff, database lock, and investigators' access to unblinded outcome data; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis. Capture each dated event as reported; approval, cutoff, or database lock does not by itself establish when investigators could see unblinded outcomes.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An SAP embedded in a protocol, supplement, or combined document is still plan Evidence when its section and scope can be located; a separate SAP file is not required. An absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

answer_anchors.text: The result follows a sufficiently detailed plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available.
The result did not follow such a pre-specified plan.
Analysis intentions or their timing are not sufficiently reported.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data. Protocol approval, ethics approval, amendment, initial registry posting, registry update, retrieval, data cutoff, and database lock are distinct events; none substitutes for the source-located date of plan finalization or investigator access to unblinded results.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent. A data cutoff or database lock is not itself proof of when investigators accessed unblinded outcomes. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results. Not establishing that a plan was early is not evidence that it was late: ground a negative chronology inference in source facts and trial circumstances, or preserve no_information when those cannot support a reasonable probable answer.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; a source-located finalization date before investigator access differs from the same plan with access timing unresolved.

A plan may be an identified section of a combined protocol or supplement. Navigate to that section and retain its exact Source and page coordinates; the lack of a separately named SAP file does not show that no plan exists.

Distinguish confidential data-monitoring access from access by trial investigators making analysis decisions. Staff providing confidential data to a monitoring committee are excepted in the official guidance; that access alone does not establish late prespecification. Public interim results are different evidence. Refining an analysis with blinded data is generally acceptable unless variables reveal intervention identity.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.

A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer. For D3.2 No, inspected context/inference or a valid scoped no-hit receipt can instead support the scoped absence of reassuring evidence; it does not assert bias occurred.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and uncertainty in inspected Evidence, scoped search receipts, or an explicit scientific limitation. Complete reading_recovery with read_pages and all context continuations. Document-structure recovery in coverage is navigation, not selected Evidence; inspect relevant unopened windows before claiming information is unreported, or retain a bounded stopping rationale. Inactive extras are ignored.

11|Summary
12|Background Optimal antiplatelet monotherapy during the chronic maintenance period in patients who undergo
13|coronary stenting is unknown. We aimed to compare head to head the efficacy and safety of aspirin and clopidogrel
14|monotherapy in this population.
15|Methods We did an investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre trial at 37 study sites in
16|South Korea. We enrolled patients aged at least 20 years who maintained dual antiplatelet therapy without clinical
17|events for 6-18 months after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents (DES). We excluded
18|patients with any ischaemic and major bleeding complications. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive a
19|monotherapy agent of clopidogrel 75 mg once daily or aspirin 100 mg once daily for 24 months. The primary endpoint
20|was a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due to acute coronary
21|syndrome, and Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) bleeding type 3 or greater, in the intention-to-treat
22|population. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02044250.
23|Findings Between March 26, 2014, and May 29, 2018, we enrolled 5530 patients. 5438 (98·3%) patients were randomly
24|assigned to either the clopidogrel group (2710 [49·8%]) or to the aspirin group (2728 [50·2%]). Ascertainment of the
25|primary endpoint was completed in 5338 (98·2%) patients. During 24-month follow-up, the primary outcome
26|occurred in 152 (5·7%) patients in the clopidogrel group and 207 (7·7%) in the aspirin group (hazard ratio 0·73
27|[95% CI 0·59-0·90]; p=0·0035).
28|Interpretation Clopidogrel monotherapy, compared with aspirin monotherapy during the chronic maintenance
29|period after percutaneous coronary intervention with DES significantly reduced the risk of the composite of all-cause
30|death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due to acute coronary syndrome, and BARC bleeding
31|type 3 or greater. In patients requiring indefinite antiplatelet monotherapy after percutaneous coronary intervention,
32|clopidogrel monotherapy was superior to aspirin monotherapy in preventing future adverse clinical events.

99|for articles published in English, with the search terms "single
100|antiplatelet therapy", "chronic maintenance", "secondary
101|prevention", "percutaneous coronary intervention", "aspirin",
102|and "clopidogrel". Our search identified two previous
103|randomised studies that investigated this issue. In the large-
104|scale CAPRIE study, which enrolled patients with
105|atherosclerotic vascular disease, clopidogrel showed a modest
106|benefit over aspirin in reducing future vascular events. In the
107|ASCET study, a smaller study that enrolled patients with
108|stable coronary artery disease on aspirin indicated for long-
109|term single antiplatelet therapy, clinical outcomes were not
110|different between aspirin and clopidogrel use. However,
111|these studies were neither done in a dedicated percutaneous
112|coronary intervention population nor done in the
113|contemporary drug-eluting stent era.
114|Added value of this study
115|The HOST-EXAM is the first randomised trial to compare
116|clopidogrel and aspirin monotherapy in patients who received
117|percutaneous coronary intervention with a drug-eluting stent.
118|In 5438 patients, clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with
119|a reduced risk of adverse clinical events (a composite of
120|all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke,
121|readmission due to acute coronary syndrome, and Bleeding
122|Academic Research Consortium bleeding of type 3 or more
123|during the 24-month follow-up period. Prespecified and
124|post-hoc subgroup analyses also showed that the beneficial
125|effect of clopidogrel monotherapy was consistent in various
126|subgroups without any significant interaction.
127|Implications of all the available evidence
128|In patients who received percutaneous coronary intervention
129|and successfully maintained the intended duration of dual
130|antiplatelet therapy, clopidogrel monotherapy was superior to
131|aspirin monotherapy in preventing future adverse clinical
132|events, including both the thrombotic composite and any
133|bleeding.

12|Randomisation and masking
13|In each participating centre, patients were randomly
14|assigned by a web-based application (MRCC IWRS
15|System; software configuration, Apache 2, PHP 5, and
16|mysql 5) developed by the MRCC (Seoul, South Korea),
17|without blocking or stratification methods. Patients who
18|met all the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion
19|criteria were randomly assigned in consecutive order
20|to either the clopidogrel group (75 mg once daily) or
21|aspirin group (100 mg once daily) in a ratio of 1:1
22|(figure 1). This study used a web-based electronic case
23|report form with the Pharmaco-epidemiology and
24|Clinical Trial Application X (PhactaX), which was
25|developed by the MRCC. When patients previously
26|using potent P2Y12 inhibitors were randomly assigned to
27|the clopidogrel group, clopidogrel 600 mg loading was
28|recommended for ticagrelor users, while prasugrel
29|users switched to clopidogrel 75 mg without a loading
30|dose. Participants and study investigators were not
31|masked to the assigned group.
32|Procedures
33|Participants received either clopidogrel (75 mg once
34|daily) or aspirin (100 mg once daily) orally. Clinical
35|follow-up was scheduled at 12 months and 24 months
36|(each with a window of plus or minus 3 months). Any
37|additional visits were at the discretion of attending
38|physicians. On each visit, active surveillance was done
39|for any adverse clinical events, along with the assessment
40|of adherence to the study drug.
41|Outcomes
42|The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death,
43|non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due
44|to acute coronary syndrome, and major bleeding
45|complications during the 24-month follow-up period.
46|Major bleeding was defined as Bleeding Academic
47|Research Consortium (BARC) type bleeding of least 3.
48|The individual components of the primary endpoint,
49|revascularisation, and minor gastrointestinal complica
50|tions were analysed as secondary endpoints at 24 months.
51|Interim analysis was not planned and was not done
52|during the follow-up duration. Post-hoc secondary com
53|posite endpoints, including the thrombotic composite
54|endpoint (defined as cardiac death, non-fatal myocardial
55|infarction, ischaemic stroke, readmission due to acute
56|coronary syndrome, and definite or probable stent
57|thrombosis) and any bleeding (defined as BARC type ≥2
58|bleeding), were analysed. Detailed definitions of each
59|clinical event are described in the appendix (pp 13-18).
60|The vital status of all patients was cross-checked through
61|the National Health Insurance Service system of South
62|Korea and the South Korea National Statistics System.
63|The definite cause of death was confirmed by the
64|recorded data classified by the International Classification
65|of Disease, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes.
66|Additionally, all source data were checked for at least
67|80% of the patients in all centres. All serious adverse
68|events, primary endpoints, and secondary endpoints

15|Between March 26, 2014, and May 29, 2018, 5530 patients

22|During the follow-up period, 35 (0·6%) patients used a
23|different antiplatelet regimen from that of the allocated
24|group, nine (0·2%) patients withdrew informed con

10|Discussion
11|The HOST-EXAM trial is the first large-scale randomised
12|controlled trial to compare clopidogrel with aspirin
13|monotherapy during the chronic maintenance period in
14|patients who received stenting with DES and had
15|successfully completed 6-18 months of DAPT without
16|events. Compared with aspirin, clopidogrel monotherapy
17|was associated with a lower risk of the composite of
18|all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke,
19|readmission due to acute coronary syndrome, and major
20|bleeding during the 24-month follow-up period. The
21|benefit of clopidogrel monotherapy was observed in both
22|thrombotic and bleeding endpoints. The results were
23|consistent across major patient subgroups, regardless
24|of baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics.
25|Also, post-hoc subgroup analyses reported no signifi
26|cant interaction between the treatment effect and
27|various subgroups, such as the DES generation, duration
28|from index PCI to randomisation, and concomitant
29|medications. Collectively, our results show that clopido
30|grel monotherapy compared with aspirin monotherapy
31|provides clinical benefit with fewer thrombotic and
32|bleeding events, when given in the chronic maintenance
33|period for patients who received PCI with DES.
34|Current practice guidelines recommend DAPT as
35|standard therapy after PCI to prevent immediate com
36|plications such as stent thrombosis and myocardial
37|infarction. After an intended duration of DAPT, clinicians
38|de-escalate to antiplatelet monotherapy during the
39|chronic maintenance phase for secondary prevention
40|of cardiovascular events. For this purpose, aspirin is
41|recommended and is the mainstay of therapy.3 Although
42|clopidogrel is used as an alternative to aspirin, especially
43|in those who are intolerant of or allergic to aspirin,
44|few studies have done a head-to-head comparison
45|between aspirin and clopidogrel in patients with stable
46|coronary artery disease. Previously, the CAPRIE trial10
47|showed that clopidogrel was moderately more effective
48|than aspirin was in reducing cardiovascular adverse
49|events in patients at risk for vascular events. Subsequent
50|studies15-17 suggested that the benefit of clopidogrel over

53|the CAPRIE trial and our study. First, the study
54|population of the CAPRIE trial was not a PCI population
55|and thus cannot represent pharmacotherapy in post-PCI
56|patients. Second, the aspirin dose in the CAPRIE trial
57|was 325 mg once daily, whereas our study used 100 mg
58|once daily. Finally, contemporary practice uses DES
59|and high-intensity statins, which were never part
60|of the CAPRIE trial because the trial was done in
61|the early 1990s. Subsequently, a few non-randomised,
62|registry-based studies compared the efficacy and safety
63|of clopidogrel with that of aspirin monotherapy for
64|secondary prevention in patients with stable coronary
65|artery disease, showing promising results for clopido
66|grel.11-13 Further, a study-level meta-analysis compared
67|P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy with aspirin mono
68|therapy for secondary prevention and concluded that
69|P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy was associated with a
70|reduced risk of myocardial infarction and a neutral
71|effect on mortality.18 Collectively, the previous studies
72|raised important hypotheses regarding which antiplatelet
73|monotherapy might yield the best clinical results in the
74|chronic maintenance period after PCI. Our study, which
75|was done in a homogeneous population of stabilised
76|patients after PCI who received DES, confirms these
77|previous findings for the first time in a large-scale
78|randomised study.
79|Two trials (the STOPDAPT-2 and SMART-CHOICE
80|trials) investigated the feasibility of P2Y12 inhibitor
81|monotherapy in patients after PCI. A meta-analysis also
82|reported that 1-3 months of DAPT followed by P2Y12
83|inhibitor monotherapy was associated with a reduced
84|risk of adverse clinical events.19 However, the major
85|difference between our study and these previous studies
86|is the timepoint at which this regimen was used.
87|Previous trials compared the efficacy and safety of P2Y12
88|inhibitor monotherapy versus DAPT within the first
89|year after PCI, whereas we compared P2Y12 inhibitor
90|monotherapy versus aspirin monotherapy 6-18 months
91|post-PCI.
92|The cumulative event curves seemed to significantly
93|diverge at 9 months. However, we saw a slight separation
94|even in the early phase and a small bump in the clopidogrel
95|group curve around 7-8 months makes it appear as
96|though the curves overlap until 9 months. Without this
97|small bump, we believe that the curves would have looked
98|as though there was a steady separation between the
99|two groups. Additionally, the cumulative incidence of
100|adverse clinical events continuously increased without
101|any plateau effect, implying a constant incidence of
102|clinical events during the chronic maintenance period
103|after PCI with DES. This finding is similar to the event
104|curve that was observed in the DAPT trial, which also
105|enrolled patients who had not had an adverse clinical
106|event within the first year after PCI.20 Moreover, we found
107|progressive divergence of the cumulative incidence curve
108|between the clopidogrel and aspirin groups, suggesting a
109|continuous benefit of clopidogrel throughout the study
110|period. Compared with the DAPT trial, the event rate in
111|our study was slightly lower despite longer follow-up
112|(18 months vs 24 months). This difference can be partially
113|explained by the fact that the DAPT trial had a much
114|higher rate of patients who received early generation DES,
115|whereas 97% of our population was treated with second
116|generation DES. Also, most of the patients in the DAPT

4|study were White, whereas our study was done in an
5|east Asian population who are known to have lower rates
6|of thrombotic events compared with those of White
7|people.21,22
8|One interesting finding from our study was that the
9|reduction of adverse clinical events, both ischaemic and
10|bleeding events, did not translate into a reduced risk of
11|death. Regarding the specific cause of death, the trend
12|of mortality rates due to cardiovascular and non-
13|cardiovascular causes were in the opposite direction
14|compared with other non-fatal outcomes, although this
15|finding was not statistically significant. Also, we found
16|numerically more cancer-related deaths in the clopidogrel
17|group than in the aspirin group. This finding could be
18|due to including more patients with unknown cancer
19|before enrolment in the clopidogrel group than in the
20|aspirin group. The protective effect of aspirin in cancer-
21|related death has been suggested in a few previous
22|studies.23,24 However, in the ASPREE trial,25 cancer-related
23|mortality occurred more frequently in healthy adults
24|who received aspirin compared to those who received
25|placebo. The influence of aspirin versus clopidogrel on
26|death (including cancer-related deaths) requires further
27|investigation and longer follow-up. We hope that the
28|extended follow-up of the HOST-EXAM trial, the so-
29|called HOST-EXAM Extended study, will bring further
30|insights on the true effect of chronic maintenance
31|monotherapy on death.
32|Our study has several limitations. First, the open-label
33|design has a potential for bias in outcome reporting
34|and ascertainment. However, all endpoints had a stan
35|dardised definition and were specifically adjudicated by
36|an independent committee that was unaware of the
37|treatment group. Second, the observed event rate of the
38|primary endpoint was lower than what was anticipated
39|in the sample size calculation, suggesting a possibility of
40|selection bias or under-reporting of events. However, we
41|periodically monitored every participating centre, where
42|imputed data were cross-checked with source documen
43|tation in more than 80% of the enrolled patients. Further,
44|the vital status of all patients randomly assigned was
45|double-checked using two national databases that have
46|access to individual mortality information. Another
47|limitation when the rate of the primary endpoint is
48|lower than expected is the possibility of a false-negative
49|result (type II error). However, our findings were
50|significant for both the primary endpoint and secondary
51|composite endpoints and the benefit of clopidogrel
52|was consistent in all prespecified subgroups. Third,
53|phenotypic and genetic testing for clopidogrel was not
54|done and the study population was east Asian patients,
55|which might limit the generalisability of the study.
56|50-60% of the east Asian population carry loss-of-
57|function mutations of the CYP2C19 gene causing an
58|attenuated antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. However,
59|multiple studies have shown that thrombotic event rates
60|are lower in east Asian people compared with in White
61|people, implying that the prognostic value of clopidogrel
62|resistance might be different between ethnicities, a
63|phenomenon termed the east Asian paradox.26 Further
64|more, drug-resistance issues are not confined to only
65|clopidogrel. In our previous study, 27 the prevalence of
66|aspirin resistance (aspirin reactivity unit >550) was
67|18·0% (164 of 911 patients), similar to 19·7% (180 of
68|911 patients) for clopidogrel resistance (platelet reactivity
69|unit >275). The clinical significance of clopidogrel
70|resistance is still under debate and current guidelines do
71|not recommend routine platelet function tests in the
72|decision making for personalised treatment approaches.3
73|Fourth, the comparison between clopidogrel and aspirin
74|for the secondary endpoints was not adjusted for multiple
75|testing and, therefore, we cannot make any definitive
76|conclusions regarding the secondary endpoints. Fifth,
77|the follow-up duration of 24 months might be too short
78|to give a concrete conclusion, considering the fact
79|that maintenance antiplatelet therapy is administered
80|indefinitely. Therefore, we have launched the HOST-
81|EXAM Extended study, in which we will be extending the
82|median follow-up to 10 years. Finally, our results only
83|apply to those who had 6-18 months of DAPT without
84|any major adverse events. Thus, extrapolation of our
85|results directly to those who use a shorter duration of
86|DAPT, such as 1 month or 3 months, is difficult. Also,
87|we cannot clearly address the optimal antiplatelet agent
88|in patients with atrial fibrillation treated with oral
89|anticoagulants.
90|In conclusion, among patients who were event free
91|for 6-18 months post-PCI and successfully received the
92|intended duration of DAPT, clopidogrel monotherapy
93|compared with aspirin monotherapy significantly
94|reduced the risk of the composite of all-cause death,
95|non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due
96|to acute coronary syndrome, and BARC type bleeding
97|of 3 or more.

Aspirin versus clopidogrel for chronic maintenance
monotherapy after percutaneous coronary intervention
(HOST-EXAM): an investigator-initiated, prospective,
randomised, open-label, multicentre trial
Bon-Kwon Koo*, Jeehoon Kang*, Kyung Woo Park*, Tae-Min Rhee, Han-Mo Yang, Ki-Bum Won, Seung-Woon Rha, Jang-Whan Bae, Nam Ho Lee,
Seung-Ho Hur, Junghan Yoon, Tae-Ho Park, Bum Soo Kim, Sang Wook Lim, Yoon Haeng Cho, Dong Woon Jeon, Sang-Hyun Kim, Jung-Kyu Han,
Eun-Seok Shin, Hyo-Soo Kim, on behalf of the HOST-EXAM investigators†
Summary
Background Optimal antiplatelet monotherapy during the chronic maintenance period in patients who undergo
coronary stenting is unknown. We aimed to compare head to head the efficacy and safety of aspirin and clopidogrel
monotherapy in this population.
Methods We did an investigator-initiated, prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre trial at 37 study sites in
South Korea. We enrolled patients aged at least 20 years who maintained dual antiplatelet therapy without clinical
events for 6-18 months after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents (DES). We excluded
patients with any ischaemic and major bleeding complications. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive a
monotherapy agent of clopidogrel 75 mg once daily or aspirin 100 mg once daily for 24 months. The primary endpoint
was a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due to acute coronary
syndrome, and Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) bleeding type 3 or greater, in the intention-to-treat
population. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02044250.
Findings Between March 26, 2014, and May 29, 2018, we enrolled 5530 patients. 5438 (98·3%) patients were randomly
assigned to either the clopidogrel group (2710 [49·8%]) or to the aspirin group (2728 [50·2%]). Ascertainment of the
primary endpoint was completed in 5338 (98·2%) patients. During 24-month follow-up, the primary outcome
occurred in 152 (5·7%) patients in the clopidogrel group and 207 (7·7%) in the aspirin group (hazard ratio 0·73
[95% CI 0·59-0·90]; p=0·0035).
Interpretation Clopidogrel monotherapy, compared with aspirin monotherapy during the chronic maintenance
period after percutaneous coronary intervention with DES significantly reduced the risk of the composite of all-cause
death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due to acute coronary syndrome, and BARC bleeding
type 3 or greater. In patients requiring indefinite antiplatelet monotherapy after percutaneous coronary intervention,
clopidogrel monotherapy was superior to aspirin monotherapy in preventing future adverse clinical events.

19|1) Background
20|Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, and
21|numerous studies have investigated its proper management and prevention. The advent of percutaneous
22|coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DESs) after antiplatelet therapy was an important
23|advance in CAD management. Previous studies proposed different antiplatelet regimens to protect
24|against thrombotic/ischemic events and minimize bleeding complications after stent implantation.
25|However, the optimal regimen after PCI with DES is still a subject of debate. Several randomized trials
26|including the RESET, OPTIMIZE, and PRODIGY have compared dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for

28|events and a higher risk of bleeding complications for longer therapy. The recent DAPT, PEGASUS-
29|TIMI, and OPTIDUAL trials reported a better efficacy of extended duration of DAPT over 12 months
30|in common, whereas the ARCTIC-Interruption trial suggested no apparent benefit but instead harm with
31|extended duration of DAPT.
